questions.problem:
Which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=\frac{1}{8}(x+4)(x+2)^{2}?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
questions.worked_solution:
The equation is already in factored form, so by the zero-product rule, we deduce that it has a single root at $x=-4$ and a double root at $x=-2.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{8}(0+4)(0+2)^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(4)(2)^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(4)(4) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,2),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-4,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-2.$

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

questions.problem:
Given that $(x+2)$ is a factor of $f(x)={x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-3x+18,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+2)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+2)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+2)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -2 & 1 & -4 & -3 & 18 \\  &  & -2 & 12 & -18 \\  & 1 & -6 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{f(x)}{x+2}={x}^{2}-6x+9
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=(x+2)({x}^{2}-6x+9).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
f(x)=(x+2)(x-3)(x-3)=(x+2)(x-3)^{2}.
$$

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=-2$ and a double root at $x=3.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(0+2)(0-3)^{2} \\  & =(2)(-3)^{2} \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,18),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-2,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=3.$

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14238854/assets/266609da7c307b98b8d5f280c75f6d8fd557c23b2e2e1885be37fa4ee3d7b229.png)

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The graph of any cubic function $y = f(x)= ax^3 + bx^2 + cx +d,$ where $a >0,$ has a characteristic inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape, with $y$-values ranging from $-\infty$ to $+\infty.$ This means that every such function has *at least* one real root and *at most* three distinct roots. 

For instance, suppose that we want to plot the graph of $y = x^3-4x^2 +4x.$ First, we need to find the roots, so we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}+4x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-4x+4) & =0 \\ x(x-2)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product rule, we get two distinct roots: $x=0$ and $x=2.$

- The root $x=0$ is a *single* root: it has multiplicity ${\color{blue}1}$ because it comes from a factor $x^{\color{blue}1}$ whose exponent is ${\color{blue}1}.$

- The root $x=2$ is a *double* root: it has multiplicity ${\color{blue}2}$ because it comes from a factor $(x-2)^{\color{blue}2}$ whose exponent is ${\color{blue}2}.$

To graph the curve, we use the following principles:

- The curve passes through the $x$-axis at the single root (in this case, $x=0$).

- The curve touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root (in this case, $x=2$).

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14238854/assets/9d3c04ff9f84bef0499b30dfd51da7efd21afe48ad323e57ff8ae9cf6a999fe7.png)
tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
The graph of any cubic function $y = f(x)= ax^3 + bx^2 + cx +d,$ where $a >0,$ has a characteristic inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape, with $y$-values ranging from $-\infty$ to $+\infty.$ This means that every such function has *at least* one real root and *at most* three distinct roots. 

For instance, suppose that we want to plot the graph of $y = x^3-4x^2 +4x.$ First, we need to find the roots, so we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}+4x & =0 \\ x({x}^{2}-4x+4) & =0 \\ x(x-2)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product rule, we get two distinct roots: $x=0$ and $x=2.$

- The root $x=0$ is a *single* root: it has multiplicity ${\color{blue}1}$ because it comes from a factor $x^{\color{blue}1}$ whose exponent is ${\color{blue}1}.$

- The root $x=2$ is a *double* root: it has multiplicity ${\color{blue}2}$ because it comes from a factor $(x-2)^{\color{blue}2}$ whose exponent is ${\color{blue}2}.$

To graph the curve, we use the following principles:

- The curve passes through the $x$-axis at the single root (in this case, $x=0$).

- The curve touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root (in this case, $x=2$).

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14238854/assets/9d3c04ff9f84bef0499b30dfd51da7efd21afe48ad323e57ff8ae9cf6a999fe7.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{3}+8{x}^{2}-16x & =0 \\ -x({x}^{2}-8x+16) & =0 \\ -x(x-4)^{2} & =0\end{aligned}

By the zero-product rule, we get two distinct roots: $x=0$ and $x=4,$ where $x=0$ is a single root and $x=4$ is a double root.

To graph the curve, we use the following principles:

- The curve passes through the $x$-axis at the single root (in this case, $x=0$).

- The curve touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root (in this case, $x=4$).
